# Part A — Creating Data Frames

## Question #1

### a. Create a vector

```{r}
student_scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)
student_scores
```

### b. Sort the scores in ascending and descending order

```{r}
# Ascending order
sort(student_scores)

# Descending order
sort(student_scores, decreasing = TRUE)
```

### c. Check if the names stayed attached to their correct values

```{r}
sorted_asc <- sort(student_scores)
sorted_asc

# Yes, the names stayed attached to their values. For example, Eli is still 67
# and Dex is still 92. Because the names are part of the vector, they move
# together with their scores when sorted.
```

### d. Create another vectors

```{r}
subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "PE")
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)

subjects
incomplete
```

### e. Sort subjects alphabetically

```{r}
sort(subjects)
```

### f. Sort incomplete using sort()

```{r}
# By default, sort() removes the NA values
sort(incomplete)

# Using na.last = TRUE keeps the NAs and places them at the end
sort(incomplete, na.last = TRUE)

# Observation: by default, sort() silently drops the two NA values without any
# warning. With na.last = TRUE, the NAs are kept and shown at the end.
```

```{r}
# Yes, the scores and names were sorted properly because I assigned them
# together, so the names are part of the scores. This is very important because
# if the names did not follow their values, the wrong person would be named the

```

# values without any warning or error. If I report "the lowest score" without
# checking for NA first, the result only reflects the students with recorded
# scores, so the dataset looks complete when it is not.

## Question #4

### a. order() compared to sort()

```{r}
order(student_scores)
sort(student_scores)

# order() returns the positions (index numbers) of the scores arranged in
# ascending order, while sort() returns the actual sorted values. In short,
# order() tells us where the values are, and sort() tells us what the values are.
```

### b. Use order() to index student_scores

```{r}
student_scores[order(student_scores)]
sort(student_scores)

identical(student_scores[order(student_scores)], sort(student_scores))

# Yes, they have the same values. order() gives the positions that arrange the
# scores in ascending order, so using them to index student_scores produces the
# same result as sort(). identical() returns TRUE, which confirms it.
```

## Question #5

### a. Create a data frame

```{r}
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio")
score <- c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74)
section <- c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")

students <- data.frame(name, score, section)
students
```

### b. Reorder the ENTIRE students data frame by score

```{r}
students[order(students$score), ]
```

### c. Reorder students by score in DESCENDING order

```{r}
students[order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

## Question #6

```{r}
order(student_scores)

# order(student_scores) returns the positions (index numbers) of the scores
# arranged in ascending order, such as 5 7 1 3 6 2 4, not the scores themselves.
# On its own, it is useless because it only tells us where the values are, not
# what they are. It becomes useful when used to index the vector, like
# student_scores[order(student_scores)], which rearranges the actual scores.
```

## Question #7

```{r, error=TRUE}
sort(student_scores)   # works, because it is a single vector
sort(students)         # error, because it is a table with several columns

# sort() only works on a single vector, so sort(students) gives an error because
# a data frame is a table of several columns and sorting a table has no clear
# meaning. order() is the correct tool because students[order(students$score), ]
# reorders every column together, keeping each row's name, score, and section
# lined up.
```

## Question #8 (rank)

### a. Use rank() and print the result

```{r}
rank(student_scores)

# Print scores and ranks side by side
cbind(scores = student_scores, rank = rank(student_scores))

# Ben and Dex both received a rank of 6.5.
```

### b. Why 6.5?

```{r}
# Ben and Dex both scored 92, so they are tied for the 6th and 7th positions.
# By default, rank() uses ties.method = "average", so each gets the average of
# those positions, (6 + 7) / 2 = 6.5. This is fair because neither student
# scored higher than the other.
```

## Question #8 (sales)

### a. Create a data frame and add the rank column

```{r}
sales <- data.frame(
  employee = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"),
  units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130)
)

# The minus sign makes the TOP seller receive rank 1
sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold)
sales
```

### b. Reorder from HIGHEST to LOWEST units_sold

```{r}
sales[order(sales$units_sold, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

## Question #9

```{r}
order(-sales$units_sold)
rank(-sales$units_sold)

# Not really. order() can reorder the table, but it only gives row positions
# (2 3 5 1 4), not each employee's standing. What it is missing is the rank
# itself and the handling of ties: rank() gives Sam and Tin 1.5 each to show
# they are tied, while order() just lists one after the other.
```
